Rubric: Accuracy 3/5 · Sourcing 2.5/5 · Usefulness 4/5 · Trust signals 2.5/5 · Engagement-fit 2/5 · Monetization integrity 3/5.
P1-VERIFIED: '899 kWh/month' — EIA FAQ: 10,791 kWh/yr ≈ 899/mo (2022 data). https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&t=3 (retrieved 2026-08-29).

P1-VERIFIED: 17-18¢/kWh band and $140-$180/mo range are consistent with EIA Electricity Monthly Update June 2026 residential average revenue 18.34¢/kWh (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/update/end-use.php, retrieved 2026-08-29); computed 899 kWh × 18.34¢ = $165/mo, inside the page's band. BUT the page's '$159/month' and '$142 was the FY2024 average' — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW against EIA Electric Power Monthly Table 5.4.a (not fetchable this run).

P1-VERIFIED (mission-critical): DOE thermostat claim verified VERBATIM — DOE Home Upgrades: 'You can save as much as 10% a year on heating and cooling by simply turning your thermostat back 7°-10°F for 8 hours a day' (https://www.energy.gov/save/home-upgrades, retrieved 2026-08-29). The page's step-1 and step-13 DOE quotes are accurate.

P1-DEFECT (mission-critical): '3–6%/degree' thermostat claim is NOT supported and internally contradicted three ways. Line 95: 'the wider 3–6%-per-degree range above' (no such per-degree range exists — the table at line 99 is per 2°F: summer 6–9% = 3.0–4.5%/deg, winter 3–5% = 1.5–2.5%/deg); FAQ line 560: 'Every 2°F change saves 3–6%' = 1.5–3.0%/deg. DOE-implied rate for an 8h setback ≈ 1.2%/degree-equivalent. Fix: keep DOE verbatim quote + the page's own 'roughly 1% per 1°F' rule of thumb; delete the '3–6%-per-degree' cross-reference at line 95 and re-label the table column 'Savings per 2°F adjustment'.

P1-DEFECT (mission-critical): RECS misattribution. Page claims standby power 'roughly 4–8% of household site-energy use (EIA RECS)' (lines 121-122, 460). RECS publishes no standby share; EIA Energy Explained puts ALL remaining end-uses (TVs, cooking, washers, dryers, electronics) at 23% of home energy (2020). The 4–8% figure may be defensible from other literature but the RECS attribution is unsupported — highest single credibility risk on the page. Fix: re-source (e.g., LBNL standby-power work) or reframe as 'electronics and small loads, ~23% (EIA)' . https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/homes.php (retrieved 2026-08-29)

P1-VERIFIED-DIRECTION: 'HVAC 40–50% of home energy use' — EIA (RECS 2020): space heating + air conditioning = 52% of household energy use; DOE: heating ≈30% of utility bill. 40–50% slightly understates — update to 'about half — 52% (EIA RECS 2020)' with the Energy Explained URL. Water-heating share '12–18%' vs DOE's 'about 20%' on the same fetched DOE page — update.

P1-DEFECT: Internal dollar contradictions Quick-Answer vs body (exact — these are reader-visible in the first screen): 'switch to LEDs ($75/year)' vs step 9 'Savings: $150–$200/year' (recomputed: 20 bulbs × ($11.17 − ~$1.70) = $189.87/yr — body is right, Quick Answer wrong); 'lower the water heater to 120°F ($40–$80/year)' vs body 'Savings: $60–$120/year'; 'kill vampire loads... ($50–$180/year)' vs step 10 'saves $120–$190/year' vs phantom section '$50–$100/year' — three ranges for one fixture.

P1-DEFECT: Water-heater math conflicts across sections: table implies 20% savings for 140→120°F ($600→$480), text says '4–7% standby loss reduction' bonus, and page 2's DOE-aligned figure is 3–5% per 10°F. Harmonize to one magnitude (recommend 3–5%/10°F per DOE guidance, i.e. ~$60/yr at the table's own $600 base).

P1-ENGAGEMENT: 87.8% bounce / 55s TOP on a 4,098-word guide. Reader hits Quick Answer → Start-here → jump-row → 3 consecutive internal-link CTA paragraphs → affiliate section before the first substantive H2. Fix: merge the three redundant CTA paragraphs (lines ~49-51 and ~63-66) into one, move 'Tools that pay for themselves' below 'Why Your Electric Bill Is So High'.

P1-TRUST: 'Nest ~12% heating / ~15% cooling (Nest product page, 2024)' and 'P3 0.2% accuracy, UL listed' — manufacturer claims properly attributed but UNVERIFIED this run → NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW (brand product/spec pages, also affiliate-disclosure coverage).

If the color shows up in the bowl, you have a leak that can probably be fixed by replacing the rubber flapper.' Page says 'check after 5–10 minutes' — align to 10 minutes and cite this URL. https://www.epa.gov/watersense/home-maintenance

P4-VERIFIED: The page's core method (read meter with all water off → wait → re-read; main-valve isolation for inside vs service-line) matches EPA's own leak-check method on the same page — and EPA adds a concrete threshold the site SHOULD adopt: 'it's likely that a family of four has a serious leak if its water use exceeds 12,000 gallons (or 16 CCF) per month during the winter.' That is the single best addition available to this page — a checkable EPA number on the site's highest-trust page.

P4-WEAK-COPY (exact quote): FAQ 'How much does a plumber cost to find a leak?' → 'Pricing varies by location, access, and the type of work required. Request an estimate from a qualified plumber before authorizing investigation or repair.' — zero-information hedging on the page's only commercial-intent question; either give an EPA/angies-type sourced national range or merge this FAQ into the responsibility question.

P4-MINOR: tags include 'therms' (a gas unit) on a water-meter page — tag pollution; remove. Also the Related-Reading link anchor '/blog/how-do-smart-meters-work/' is used in body as 'how water meters work and how accurate they are' — anchor/target mismatch (electric-meter slug), verify intent.
